claim: Computational modeling of behavior has revolutionized psychology and neuroscience.

claim: By fitting models to experimental data we can probe the algorithms underlying behavior.

claim: By fitting models to experimental data we can find neural correlates of computational variables.

claim: Behavioral data most often come in the form of choices.
source: The behavioral data most often come in the form of choices, but can also be reaction times, eye movements, or other easily observable behaviors, and even neural data.
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field, based on established knowledge.

claim: Behavioral data can also be reaction times, eye movements, or other easily observable behaviors, and even neural data.

claim: Computational models instantiate different 'algorithmic hypotheses' about how behavior is generated.

evidence: This is a conceptual statement about what computational models represent, based on established understanding.

claim: What it means to 'make sense' of behavioral data will vary according to the researcher's goals.
source: Exactly what it means to 'make sense' of behavioral data is, to some extent, a matter of taste that will vary according to the researcher's goals (Kording et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kording et al., 2018.

claim: In some cases, a simple model that can explain broad qualitative features of the data is enough.
source: In some cases, a simple model that can explain broad qualitative features of the data is enough. In other cases, more detailed models that make quantitative predictions are required (Breiman, 2001).
evidence: This describes different modeling approaches, supported by citation to Breiman, 2001.

claim: In other cases, more detailed models that make quantitative predictions are required.

claim: Four uses dominate the literature: simulation, parameter estimation, model comparison, and latent variable inference.
source: The exact form of the models, and exactly what we do with them, is limited only by our imaginations, but four uses dominate the literature: simulation, parameter estimation, model comparison, and latent variable inference.
evidence: This is a statement about common practices in the field, based on established knowledge.

claim: Each of these uses can be mishandled in a number of ways, causing us to draw wrong and misleading conclusions.

claim: Modeling is particularly popular in the field of learning.

claim: The field of learning benefits from modeling particularly because of the nature of the behavioral data: trials are dependent on all past history and thus unique, making classic data analysis with aggregation across conditions less successful.

claim: Computational modeling can never replace good experimental design.

claim: Modeling is fundamentally limited by the behavioral data, which is itself fundamentally limited by the experimental protocol.

claim: The best experiments make the processes of interest identifiable in classical analyses of the behavioral data.

claim: Computational modeling is rarely informative when there is no evidence of an effect in model-independent analyses of behavior.

claim: Code for implementing all of the examples is available on GitHub.

claim: Bad models can limit the conclusions we can draw.
source: Just as bad experiments can limit our ability to test different hypotheses, bad models – quite literally the mathematical embodiment of our hypotheses – can further limit the conclusions we can draw (Donkin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Donkin et al., 2014.

claim: Even well-established computational models can be problematic in some cases.
source: This point is especially important if we are designing new models, but even well-established computational models can be problematic in some cases (Broomell and Bhatia, 2014; Nilsson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Broomell and Bhatia, 2014; Nilsson et al., 2011.

claim: Computational modelers have a wide variety of goals for their models.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kording et al., 2018.

claim: The delta rule was first invented using a heuristics approach.

claim: Algorithms such as Q-learning and temporal difference learning have been related to human and animal behavior and brain function.

claim: Ideal observer models in vision are an example where the Bayes-optimal perspective has been applied successfully.

claim: Formal model comparison techniques include a penalty for overly complex models.
source: Indeed, formal model comparison techniques (described in detail in Appendix 2) include a penalty for overly complex models, which are more likely to overfit the data and generalize poorly, and favor simpler models so long as they can account for the data.
evidence: This describes a property of formal model comparison techniques, based on established knowledge.

claim: Finding qualitative signatures of the model is crucial.

By studying these measures with simulated data, you will have greater intuition about what is going on when you use the same model-independent measures to analyze real behavior (Daw et al., 2011; Collins and Frank, 2012; Collins and Frank, 2013; Nassar et al., 2018; Lee and Webb, 2005).

claim: A brute force search of the entire parameter space is occasionally useful.

claim: Brute force search is unfeasible outside of the simplest cases because of the high computational costs.

evidence: This describes a limitation of brute force search, based on established knowledge in optimization.

claim: A key limitation of optimization algorithms is that they are only guaranteed to find local minima, which are not guaranteed to be the global minima.
source: Finally, a key limitation of optimization algorithms is that they are only guaranteed to find local minima, which are not guaranteed to be the global minima corresponding to the best fitting parameters.
evidence: This describes a fundamental limitation of optimization algorithms, based on established knowledge in optimization theory.

claim: Parameter recovery is a crucial part of any model-based analysis.
source: Such a procedure is known as 'Parameter Recovery', and is a crucial part of any model-based analysis.
evidence: This is a normative statement about best practices in model-based analysis, based on established knowledge.

claim: Even successful parameter recovery represents a best-case scenario.
source: Remember that even successful parameter recovery represents a best-case scenario!
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of parameter recovery, based on understanding of the method.

claim: The 'true' generative process for behavior is likely much more complex than any model you could conceive.
source: This is the best case you could possibly hope for in the model-based analysis and it is unlikely to ever occur as the 'true' generative process for behavior — that is, the inner workings of the mind and brain — is likely much more complex than any model you could conceive.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the complexity of cognitive processes, based on general understanding.

claim: Overfitting decreases the generalizability of the model.
source: Overfitting is a problem in that it decreases the generalizability of the model: it makes it less likely that the conclusions drawn would apply to a different sample.
evidence: This describes a consequence of overfitting, based on established knowledge in statistics and machine learning.

claim: Cross-validation avoids overfitting by measuring fit on held-out data.
source: One way to avoid overfitting is to perform cross-validation: by measuring fit on held-out data, we directly test generalizability.
evidence: This describes a method for avoiding overfitting, based on established knowledge in statistics and machine learning.

claim: Model comparison should be validated by model recovery on simulated data.
source: Just as parameter fitting should be validated by parameter recovery on simulated data, so model comparison should be validated by model recovery on simulated data.
evidence: This is a normative statement about best practices in model comparison, based on established knowledge.

claim: Model comparison only tells you which of the models you considered fits the data best.
source: As wonderful as it is to find that your model 'best' fits the behavioral data, the elephant in the room (or perhaps more correctly not in the room) with all model comparison is that it only tells you which of the models you considered fits the data best.
evidence: This describes a fundamental limitation of model comparison, based on established knowledge.

claim: If the model-independent analyses do not show evidence of the expected results, there is almost no point in fitting the model.
source: If the model-independent analyses do not show evidence of the expected results, there is almost no point in fitting the model.
evidence: This is a normative statement about when to proceed with model fitting, based on the authors' experience and understanding.

claim: If there is no model-independent evidence that the processes of interest are engaged, then a model-based analysis is unlikely to uncover evidence for the processes either.
source: In our experience, if there is no model-independent evidence that the processes of interest are engaged, then a model-based analysis is unlikely to uncover evidence for the processes either.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experience, representing empirical observation.

claim: Human behavior is always messier than the model.
source: An important point to remember is that human behavior is always messier than the model, and it is unlikely that the class of models you explored actually contains the 'real' model thatgenerated human behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about the relationship between models and behavior, based on established understanding.

claim: It is unlikely that the class of models you explored actually contains the 'real' model that generated human behavior.

claim: Modeling unimportant parameters usually captures variance in the behavior that would otherwise be attributed to noise.
source: Modeling these unimportant parameters usually captures variance in the behavior that would otherwise be attributed to noise, and as such, makes for a better estimation of 'important' parameters.
evidence: This is an inference about the benefits of modeling additional parameters, based on understanding of statistical modeling.

claim: Model validation should never be skipped.
source: This step is called model validation, and should never be skipped: it is possible to fit a model, get high fit measures, and nevertheless completely miss the essence of the behavior.
evidence: This is a normative statement about best practices in model-based analysis, based on established knowledge.

claim: It is possible to fit a model, get high fit measures, and nevertheless completely miss the essence of the behavior.

claim: Interpreting average trial likelihood as an absolute measure of fit is of limited value when choices are stochastic or the environment is complex.
source: Although this measure has some nice properties — for example, the best possible value is one when the model predicts behavior perfectly — it offers limited value when choices are actually stochastic (which may be the case in many situations; Drugowitsch et al., 2016) or the environment is complex.
evidence: This describes a limitation of using average trial likelihood, with citation to Drugowitsch et al., 2016 about stochastic choices.

claim: A better method to validate a model is to simulate it with the fit parameter values.
source: A better method to validate a model is to simulate it with the fit parameter values (Palminteri et al., 2017; Nassar and Frank, 2016; Navarro, 2019), a procedure long performed by statisticians as part of the 'posterior predictive check' (Roecker, 1991; Gelman et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple sources recommending this approach.

claim: Palminteri and colleagues offer a striking example where Model A fits better than Model B by any quantitative measure of model comparison, but is completely unable to capture the essence of the behavior.
source: Palminteri and colleagues (Palminteri et al., 2017) offer a striking example of this effect, where Model A fits better than Model B by any quantitative measure of model comparison, but is completely unable to capture the essence of the behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Palminteri et al., 2017.

claim: Model-dependent analyses should only be performed on the winning model.
source: To minimize risks of p-hacking, model-dependent analyses should only be performed on the winning model, after researchers are satisfied that the model captures the behavior.
evidence: This is a normative statement about best practices to avoid p-hacking, based on established understanding.

claim: Latent variables are the hidden components of the algorithms underlying the behavior that are not directly observable from the behavior itself.
source: Latent variables are the hidden components of the algorithms underlying the behavior that are not directly observable from the behavior itself.
evidence: This is a definition of latent variables, based on established knowledge.

claim: If we are to take the model seriously, latent variables should have some representation in the subjects' mind and brain.
source: These latent variables shed light on the internal workings of the model and, if we are to take the model seriously, should have some representation in the subjects' mind and brain (Cohen et al., 2017; O'Doherty et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cohen et al., 2017; O'Doherty et al., 2007.

claim: The simplest approach to combining latent variables with physiological data uses linear regression to test whether physiological variables correlate with the latent variables of interest.
source: The simplest of these approaches uses linear regression to test whether physiological variables correlate with the latent variables of interest. Such an approach has led to a number of insights into the neural mechanisms underlying behavior (Nassar et al., 2012; Daw et al., 2011; Donoso et al., 2014; Collins and Frank, 2018; Fischer and Ullsperger, 2013), although, as with any modeling exercise, latent variable analysis should be done with care (Wilson and Niv, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies using this approach, with a cautionary citation to Wilson and Niv, 2015.

claim: Latent variable analysis should be done with care.

claim: Fit parameters can be treated as a dependent variable in continuous analyses.

claim: Exceedance probabilities are a more sophisticated and less biased way to report model comparison results.

claim: The method of Rigoux et al. (2014) computes Exceedance Probabilities.

claim: With good priors, MAP parameters can be more accurate than parameters estimated with maximum likelihood approaches.

claim: When the priors are bad, MAP estimation has problems of its own.

claim: Hierarchical Bayesian approaches make it possible to fit all participants simultaneously, integrating assumptions about their dependence.
